slots.text: So the knight makes the movement — but which movement? Will he forget the whole thing — for there is a kind of concentration in that too, is there not? No! For the knight does not contradict himself, and it is a contradiction to forget all that one’s life contained and still remain the same. He has no urge to become someone else, and he by no means considers that the great thing. Only the lower natures forget themselves and become something new. The butterfly, for instance, has entirely forgotten that it was a caterpillar; perhaps it can in turn forget so entirely that it was a butterfly that it can become a fish. The deeper natures never forget themselves; they never turn into anything but what they were. So the knight will remember everything; but this remembering is precisely the pain, and yet in infinite resignation he is reconciled with existence. For him, his love for that princess became the expression of an eternal love. It took on a religious character; it was transfigured into a love for the eternal being — who did, it is true, deny the fulfillment, but who nevertheless reconciled him again in the eternal consciousness that his love is valid in a form of eternity that no actuality can take from him. Fools and young people prattle that for a human being everything is possible. But this is a grave error. In terms of spirit, all things are possible; but in the world of finitude a great deal is not. Yet the knight makes this impossibility possible by expressing it spiritually — and he expresses it spiritually by renouncing it. The wish that would have led him out into actuality, but was wrecked on the impossibility, is now bent inward; yet that does not mean it is lost, nor is it forgotten. Sometimes it is the dim stirrings of the wish within him that awaken the memory; sometimes he awakens it himself. For he is too proud to want what was the whole content of his life to have been the affair of a fleeting moment. He keeps this love young, and it grows with him in years and in beauty. Yet he needs no finite occasion to make it grow. From the moment he has made the movement, the princess is lost. He has no need of those erotic tremblings of the nerves at the sight of the beloved, and so on. Nor does he need, in the finite sense, to be forever taking leave of her, because in the eternal sense he remembers her. And he knows very well that lovers who are so keen to see each other once more, in farewell, for the last time, are right to be keen, and right to think that it is the last time; for they are the ones who forget each other soonest. He has understood the deep secret that even in loving another human being one ought to be sufficient to oneself. He no longer takes any finite account of what the princess does, and that is exactly the proof that he has made the movement infinitely. This is where one can get to see whether the movement in the single individual is true or feigned. Someone else, too, believed he had made the movement; but, look, time went on, and the princess did something else — married a prince, for instance — and then his soul lost the elasticity of resignation. By this he showed that he had not made the movement correctly; for whoever has resigned infinitely is sufficient to himself. The knight does not cancel his resignation. He preserves his love as young as it was in its first moment; he never lets it slip from him, precisely because he has made the movement infinitely. Nothing the princess does can disturb him. Only the lower natures find the law for their actions in another human being — the premises of their actions outside themselves. If, on the other hand, the princess is of a like mind, then something beautiful will come of it. She will then introduce herself into that order of knighthood into which no one is admitted by ballot, but of which everyone is a member who has the courage to introduce himself — the order of knighthood that proves its immortality by making no distinction between man and woman. She, too, will preserve her love young and healthy; she, too, will have got over her anguish, even if she does not, as the old song has it, “lie every night at her lord’s side.” These two will then suit each other for all eternity, with a harmonia praestabilita — a pre-established harmony — so perfectly in time that if ever the moment came (a moment that does not, however, occupy them in the finite sense, for then they would grow old), if ever the moment came that allowed their love to be given its expression in time, they would be able to begin exactly where they would have begun if they had been united from the start. Anyone who understands this, man or woman, can never be deceived; for only the lower natures imagine that they have been deceived. No girl who is not this proud really knows how to love; but if she is this proud, then all the cunning and cleverness in the world cannot deceive her.

In infinite resignation there is peace and rest. Every human being who wills it — who has not debased himself by holding himself in contempt, which is even more terrible than being too proud — can train himself to make this movement, which, in its pain, reconciles a person to existence. Infinite resignation is that shirt spoken of in an old folk tale. The thread is spun under tears, bleached with tears, the shirt sewn in tears; but then it also protects better than iron and steel. The imperfection in the folk tale is that a third party can make up this linen. The secret of life is that everyone has to sew it for himself; and the remarkable thing is that a man can sew it every bit as well as a woman. In infinite resignation there is peace and rest and consolation in pain — provided, that is, the movement is made normally. I could, however, easily write a whole book if I set out to go through the various misunderstandings, the back-to-front positions, the sloppy movements I have come across in my own small practice alone. People believe very little in spirit; and yet it is precisely spirit that matters in making this movement. What matters is that the movement not be the one-sided result of a dira necessitas — a harsh necessity — and the more that necessity is present, the more doubtful it always becomes whether the movement is normal. So if one means to hold that cold, barren necessity must necessarily be present in the movement, one is thereby saying that no one can experience death before he really dies — and that strikes me as crass materialism. But in our time people care less about making pure movements. Suppose someone who was to learn dancing said: “Generation upon generation has now spent centuries learning the positions; it is high time I turned this to my advantage and started straight in on the française.” People would probably laugh at him a little; but in the world of spirit this is found extremely plausible. What, then, is cultivation? I thought it was the course the single individual runs through in order to catch up with himself; and whoever will not go through this course is helped very little by having been born in the most enlightened age.

Infinite resignation is the final stage preceding faith, so that whoever has not made this movement is without faith. For it is only in infinite resignation that I become clear to myself in my eternal validity, and not until then can there be talk of grasping existence by virtue of faith.

Let us now have the knight of faith appear in the case described. He does precisely what the other knight does. He gives up, infinitely, the love that is his life’s content, and he is reconciled in the pain. But then the marvel occurs: he makes yet another movement, more wondrous than anything, for he says: “I believe nevertheless that I will get her — by virtue, that is, of the absurd, by virtue of this: that for God everything is possible.” The absurd does not belong among the distinctions that lie within the understanding’s own range. It is not the same thing as the improbable, the unexpected, the unlooked-for. At the moment the knight resigned, he assured himself of the impossibility, humanly speaking; this was the understanding’s result, and he had energy enough to think it. In the infinite sense, on the other hand, it was possible — namely, by resigning it. But to possess it in this way is, of course, at the same time to give it up; and yet for the understanding such possessing is no absurdity. For the understanding went on being right that in the world of wretchedness where it rules, it was and remained an impossibility. The knight of faith is just as clearly conscious of this. Accordingly, nothing can save him but the absurd, and this he grasps by faith. He acknowledges the impossibility, then, and in the same moment he believes the absurd. For if he wants to imagine that he has faith without acknowledging the impossibility with all the passion of his soul and with his whole heart, he deceives himself, and his testimony has no footing anywhere, since he has not even come as far as infinite resignation.

Faith is therefore not an aesthetic emotion (the aesthetic being the sphere of immediate feeling) but something far higher, precisely because resignation comes before it. It is not the immediate impulse of the heart, but the paradox of existence. So when a young girl, in spite of all difficulties, nevertheless remains certain that her wish will indeed be fulfilled, this certainty is not at all the certainty of faith — even though she has been brought up by Christian parents and has perhaps gone to the pastor for instruction for a whole year. She is certain in all her childlike naivety and innocence. This certainty, too, ennobles her being and gives her a supernatural stature, so that like a thaumaturge — a worker of wonders — she can conjure the finite powers of existence and bring even stones to weep; while, on the other hand, in her fluster she is as likely to run to Herod as to Pilate, touching all the world with her pleading. Her certainty is most lovable, and one can learn much from her; but there is one thing one does not learn from her: one does not learn to make movements. For her certainty does not dare to look the impossibility in the eye, in the pain of resignation.

I can understand, then, that making the infinite movement of resignation requires strength and energy and freedom of spirit; I can also understand that it is feasible. The next thing astonishes me; my brain turns over in my head. For after having made the movement of resignation, then by virtue of the absurd to get everything — to get the wish, whole and undiminished — that is beyond human powers; it is a marvel. But this I can understand: that the young girl’s certainty is mere light-mindedness compared with the unshakability of faith, even though faith’s unshakability has seen the impossibility. Every time I want to make this movement, everything goes black before my eyes; in the same moment I admire it absolutely, and in the same moment a tremendous anxiety seizes my soul — for what, then, is tempting God? And yet this movement is the movement of faith, and it goes on being so, even if philosophy, to confuse the concepts, would have us believe that it has faith, and even if theology wants to sell it off cheap.

No faith is needed in order to resign. For what I win in resignation is my eternal consciousness; that is a purely philosophical movement, one I am confident I can make when it is demanded, and one I can discipline myself to make. For every time some bit of finitude threatens to get the better of me, I starve myself out until I make the movement; for my eternal consciousness is my love of God, and that ranks higher for me than anything. No faith is needed in order to resign; but faith is needed in order to get the very least thing more than my eternal consciousness, for this is what is paradoxical. The movements are often confused. People say that one needs faith in order to renounce everything. Indeed, one hears something stranger still: a person complains that he has lost his faith, and when one checks the scale to see where he stands on it, one sees, strangely enough, that he has only reached the point at which he ought to make the infinite movement of resignation. In resignation I renounce everything. I make this movement on my own; and if I fail to make it, that is because I am cowardly and effete and lacking in enthusiasm, and have no feeling for the significance of the lofty dignity allotted to every human being: that of being his own censor — a far more distinguished office than being censor general of the entire Roman Republic. I make this movement on my own, and what I thereby win is myself in my eternal consciousness, in blessed understanding with my love for the eternal being. By faith I renounce nothing; on the contrary, by faith I get everything — precisely in the sense in which it is said that whoever has faith as a grain of mustard seed can move mountains. A purely human courage is needed to renounce all of temporality in order to win eternity. But eternity I do win, and I can never in all eternity renounce it; that would be a self-contradiction. But a paradoxical and humble courage is needed to grasp, after that, the whole of temporality by virtue of the absurd — and this courage is faith’s. By faith Abraham did not give Isaac up; by faith Abraham got Isaac. By virtue of resignation that rich young man ought to have given everything away; but when he had done so, the knight of faith should have said to him: “By virtue of the absurd you will get every last penny back, provided you can believe it.” And these words ought by no means to be a matter of indifference to the formerly rich young man; for if he gave his possessions away because he was sick of them, then his resignation was in a sorry state.

Temporality, finitude — that is what everything turns on. By my own powers I can resign everything, and then find peace and rest in pain. I can bear everything — even if that dreadful demon, more terrible than the skeleton Death who frightens people — even if madness held up the fool’s costume before my eyes and I understood from its look that it was I who was to put it on. I can still save my soul, as long as it matters more to me that my love for God should triumph in me than that I should have earthly happiness. Even in this last moment a person can gather his whole soul in one single glance toward the heaven from which every good gift comes; and this glance will be understood, by him and by the one it seeks, to mean that he stayed true to his love after all. Then he will calmly put on the costume. Anyone whose soul lacks this romance has sold his soul, whether he got a kingdom for it or a miserable piece of silver. But by my own powers I cannot get the least of what belongs to finitude; for I am constantly using my powers to resign everything. By my own powers I can give up the princess, and I will not become a sulker; I will find joy and peace and rest in my pain. But by my own powers I cannot get her back, for it is precisely to resign that I am using my powers. But by faith, says that wonderful knight — by faith you will get her, by virtue of the absurd.

This movement, you see, I cannot make. As soon as I want to begin on it, everything turns upside down, and I flee back into the pain of resignation. I can swim in life, but for this mystical hovering I am too heavy. To exist so that at every moment my opposition to existence expresses itself as the most beautiful and secure harmony with it — that I cannot do. And yet it must be glorious to get the princess. I say so at every moment, and the knight of resignation who does not say so is a fraud: he has not had a single wish, and he has not kept the wish young in his pain. Perhaps there was one who found it convenient enough that the wish was no longer alive, that the arrow of pain had been blunted; but someone like that is no knight. A free-born soul who caught himself at it would despise himself and start over, and above all would not let his soul be deceived by itself. And yet it must be glorious to get the princess. And yet only the knight of faith is happy — the hereditary lord of the finite — while the knight of resignation is a stranger and a foreigner. For it was conceivable too, of course, that the knight of resignation might get the princess; but his soul had seen through the impossibility of their future happiness. No — to get the princess in this way, to live happily and joyfully day in and day out with her; in this way to live happily and joyfully every moment by virtue of the absurd, at every moment to see the sword hovering above the head of the beloved, and yet to find not rest in the pain of resignation but joy by virtue of the absurd — that is wonderful. Whoever does it is great, the only great one. The thought of it moves my soul, which was never stingy in admiring what is great.

Suppose, now, that everyone of my own time who will not stop at faith really is a man who has comprehended the horror of life, who has understood what Daub means when he says that a soldier standing alone at his post with a loaded rifle, by a powder magazine, on a stormy night, gets strange thoughts. Suppose that everyone who will not stop at faith really is a man who had the strength of soul to comprehend the thought that the wish was an impossibility, and who then took time to be alone with that thought. Suppose that everyone who will not stop at faith is a man who was reconciled in pain and reconciled by pain. Suppose that everyone who will not stop at faith is a man who then (and if he has not done all of the foregoing, he need not trouble himself when faith is under discussion) did the wonderful thing and grasped the whole of existence by virtue of the absurd. Then what I am writing is the highest eulogy on my contemporaries, by the least among them — one who could make only the movement of resignation. But in that case why will people not stop at faith? Why does one sometimes hear that people are embarrassed to confess that they have faith? This I cannot comprehend. If I ever get so far as to be able to make this movement, then from that day on I shall drive a coach and four.

Is it really so? Is all the philistinism I see in life — which I let be judged not by my word but by my deed — really not what it seems? Is it the marvel? That is conceivable, after all; for that hero of faith did bear a striking resemblance to it — since that hero of faith was not even an ironist and humorist, but something still higher. There is a great deal of talk in our time about irony and humor, especially from people who have never managed to practice them, but who nonetheless know how to explain everything. I am not wholly a stranger to these two passions; I know somewhat more about them than is to be found in German and German-Danish compendiums. So I know that these two passions differ essentially from the passion of faith. Irony and humor also turn their reflection on themselves, and therefore belong in the sphere of infinite resignation; their elasticity lies in the individual’s being incommensurable with actuality.

The last movement, the paradoxical movement of faith, I cannot make — be it a duty or whatever it may be — although I would be only too glad to. Whether a person has the right to say this must be left to him; it becomes a matter between him and the eternal being who is the object of faith, whether he can come to an amicable settlement on this point. What every human being can do is make the movement of infinite resignation; and I for my part would not hesitate to call anyone a coward who wants to imagine that he cannot. With faith it is another matter. But what no human being has the right to do is to talk others into imagining that faith is a small thing, or an easy matter, when it is the greatest and the hardest thing of all.

People take the story of Abraham another way. They praise God’s grace for granting him Isaac again — the whole thing was only a test. A test — this word can say a lot or a little, and yet the whole business is over the moment it is said. One climbs onto a winged horse; in the same instant one is on Mount Moriah; in the same instant one sees the ram. One forgets that Abraham rode only on a donkey, which goes slowly along the road; that he had a three-day journey; that he needed some time to split the firewood, to bind Isaac and to sharpen the knife.

And yet people praise Abraham. The one who is to speak can quite well sleep until the last quarter of an hour before he has to speak; the listener can quite well fall asleep during the speech; for everything goes easily enough, without trouble on either side. If there were a man present who suffered from sleeplessness, then perhaps he went home, sat down in a corner and thought: “The whole thing is a matter of a moment. Just wait a minute and you will see the ram, and the test is over.” If the speaker came upon him in this state, I imagine he would plant himself before him in all his dignity and say: “You wretch, that you can let your soul sink into such foolishness! No miracle happens, and the whole of life is a test.” As the speaker went on with his outpouring, he got more and more worked up and grew more and more pleased with himself; and whereas he had noticed no rush of blood to the head while he was speaking about Abraham, he now felt the vein swelling in his forehead. Perhaps he would be struck dumb if the sinner answered calmly and with dignity: “But that is what you preached about last Sunday.”

So let us either strike Abraham out altogether, or let us learn to be horrified at the tremendous paradox that is the meaning of his life, so that we may understand that our time, like every time, can be glad if it has faith. If Abraham is not a nullity, a phantom, a bauble one plays with to pass the time, then the error can never lie in the sinner’s wanting to do the same. What matters is to see how great a thing it was that Abraham did, so that the man can judge for himself whether he has the calling and the courage to be put to the proof in such a thing. The comic contradiction in the speaker’s conduct was that he made Abraham into something insignificant, and yet wanted to forbid the other man to behave in the same way.

Should one, then, not dare to speak about Abraham? I rather think one should. If I had to speak about him, I would begin by portraying the pain of the test. For this purpose I would suck, leech-like, every bit of anxiety and distress and torment out of a father’s suffering, so that I could describe what Abraham suffered while through it all he nevertheless had faith. I would point out that the journey took three days and a good way into the fourth; indeed, those three and a half days should become infinitely longer than the couple of thousand years that separate me from Abraham. Then I would point out — for this is my opinion — that every human being still dares to turn around before he begins on such a thing, and can at any moment turn back in repentance. If this is done, I fear no danger, nor do I fear arousing in people a wish to be put to the proof as Abraham was. But if one wants to sell off a cut-price edition of Abraham, and yet forbid everyone to do the same, then it is ridiculous.

It is now my intention, then, to draw out from the story of Abraham, in the form of problemata — questions set for debate — the dialectical element that lies in it, in order to see what a tremendous paradox faith is: a paradox capable of turning a murder into a holy act, pleasing to God; a paradox that returns Isaac to Abraham, which no thinking can master, because faith begins precisely where thinking leaves off.
